frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains a major market for Algerian gas, giving Algiers leverage but also exposing revenues and infrastructure plans to shifts in European energy policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's effort to preserve strategic autonomy from outside military powers.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Debt and Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed transport and energy infrastructure remains strategically important, while debt-servicing demands constrain Luanda's room to capture full value from resource exports.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Western and Gulf-backed interest in the Lobito Corridor creates opportunities for diversification but risks leaving Angola primarily as a transit and extraction platform for copper, cobalt, and critical minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border and Transit Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted established trade routes and exposed Benin's dependence on regional transit arrangements beyond its direct control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Port and Logistics Capital
frictionVectors.details: External investment is strengthening Cotonou's logistics role, but foreign participation in port, digital, and industrial infrastructure creates long-term leverage over national supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains significant leverage in diamond governance, but negotiations over marketing, sorting, and beneficiation remain central to preserving domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Risk
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other critical minerals could reduce diamond dependence, provided new projects do not reproduce enclave-style extraction with limited local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal Gold and Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Gold is increasingly framed as a sovereign financing asset, but informal mining, smuggling networks, and insecurity limit the state's ability to capture revenues and regulate production.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from French and Western security ties toward Russian support may expand junta autonomy, while sanctions exposure and opaque security-linked resource arrangements create new external vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Border Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Relations remain strained by accusations of rebel support and border insecurity, disrupting trade and limiting regional cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral exports remain vulnerable to informal channels and foreign intermediaries, reducing state capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Port and Connectivity Assets
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, digital, and tourism infrastructure depend heavily on European, Chinese, and multilateral capital, limiting full domestic control over strategic nodes.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago faces persistent risks from Atlantic narcotics trafficking and illegal fishing, requiring sustained external security cooperation.

highlights: Oil and mining rents remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and lenders remain central to oil, mining, rail, port, and pipeline development, giving outside actors substantial leverage over export corridors and revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Separatist Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts agriculture, transport, and public administration while creating openings for illicit cross-border networks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain influence around regime protection and mineral access, complicating transparent licensing and national revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Exposed Transport Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and insecurity leave trade routes and mining zones dependent on armed protection, neighboring states, and external humanitarian logistics.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a centralized state

frictionVectors.title: Oil Corridor and Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The export pipeline and upstream oil sector remain dependent on foreign operators and infrastructure, constraining N'Djamena's control over pricing, investment, and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: France's reduced role, Russian outreach, and regional instability are intensifying competition over military access and political influence while Chad manages conflict spillovers from Sudan and the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty grievance and limits Comoros' control over surrounding maritime space. The dispute periodically sharpens diplomatic tensions and complicates regional migration management.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, foreign aid, and externally financed infrastructure, giving France, Gulf partners, and other donors influence over national priorities. Limited state capacity constrains independent development of fisheries and offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to undermine Kinshasa's control over territory, transport corridors, and mineral-producing areas. Rwanda-linked security dynamics and wider regional competition remain major threats to sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Bargains and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western actors compete for access to cobalt, copper, lithium, and other strategic minerals. Weak oversight, opaque contracts, and transport bottlenecks reduce the state's ability to capture full value from its resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state's fiscal position remains highly exposed to oil prices and offshore production controlled through partnerships with international energy companies. This limits diversification and leaves public investment vulnerable to external market conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and contractors remain important to roads, public works, and extractive infrastructure. Debt obligations and limited transparency can narrow policy autonomy while channeling gains toward external firms and creditors.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Resource Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and trading houses retain substantial influence over cocoa, gold, oil, and emerging mineral value chains. Abidjan is strengthening local processing and state regulation, but external capital still captures significant value.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover Risk
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Burkina Faso and Mali places pressure on northern borders, trade routes, and security spending. Expanded foreign security cooperation improves resilience but can create new dependencies and political sensitivities.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Base Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position beside the Bab el-Mandeb through US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The arrangement generates revenue and security guarantees but constrains strategic autonomy and raises exposure to regional conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: External financing and management of ports, logistics, and transport links—especially those connected to Ethiopia—remain central to the economy. Debt exposure and contested infrastructure deals limit the state's control over long-term strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and major Gulf investments provide essential liquidity but increase outside influence over strategic assets, land, and monetary policy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and canal security
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and instability around the Red Sea continue to threaten Suez Canal revenues and compel costly maritime-security coordination with external powers.

highlights: China remains a key infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil output and limited diversification weaken fiscal sovereignty, leaving the state exposed to foreign energy firms, commodity prices, and shrinking export rents.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-access dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and lending remain important to national infrastructure, creating long-term exposure to external contractors and commercial leverage.

highlights: Mining remains the main foreign-currency channel

frictionVectors.title: Mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide hard currency but concentrate resource control in state-linked and foreign mining arrangements with limited transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia, Sudan, and the Red Sea keep Eritrea strategically exposed and encourage security relationships that can constrain independent policymaking.

frictionVectors.title: South African dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport corridors, markets, electricity links, and customs arrangements, limiting autonomous control over supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal and governance pressure
frictionVectors.details: Public-finance constraints and political tensions complicate investment diversification and increase dependence on regional lenders and preferential trade regimes.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access contest
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's push for dependable maritime access, especially through Somaliland or other regional arrangements, is a major source of friction with Somalia and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on external financing constrain sovereignty over major infrastructure, while conflict-related disruptions continue to threaten domestic resource mobilization.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transition government is pressing foreign mining and logistics operators for greater local value capture, especially in manganese and related infrastructure. This improves bargaining power but risks investor pullback and contract disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Railway and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon’s mineral exports depend heavily on the Transgabon railway and coastal terminals, leaving sovereign resource control vulnerable to foreign capital, maintenance gaps, and logistical bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access and weak monitoring continue to constrain Gambian control over marine resources. Local fishers face declining stocks while enforcement remains dependent on limited state capacity and external support.

frictionVectors.title: Port and transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies on regional trade corridors and Senegal-linked infrastructure, limiting its autonomy over transport and customs revenues. Banjul’s modernization needs also create openings for foreign lenders and operators.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and water security
frictionVectors.details: Informal and politically connected gold mining continues to damage farmland and water systems, weakening state control over a strategic export. Efforts to formalize the sector face resistance from entrenched local and commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions narrow Accra’s room to subsidize infrastructure and retain greater resource rents. Ghana is seeking stronger domestic processing and state participation while managing investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium control
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore and rail-port complex offers major fiscal gains but remains dependent on large foreign-led consortia, imported expertise, and long-term infrastructure agreements. Conakry must balance revenue demands against the risk of delayed investment.

frictionVectors.title: Junta transition uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Political uncertainty and delayed civilian normalization complicate contract credibility and access to international finance. The authorities use mining nationalism to build legitimacy, but opaque renegotiations can reduce sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most of its cashew crop with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign traders and price swings. Efforts to develop processing capacity remain constrained by weak electricity, finance, and institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and political instability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau’s port and customs systems remain vulnerable to patronage, external commercial influence, and recurring political disruption. Limited administrative capacity reduces the government’s ability to secure strategic infrastructure and capture resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is strengthening control over the Mombasa–Northern Corridor, but Gulf, Chinese, and regional investment remains influential in ports, logistics, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure limits fiscal room and increases sensitivity to lenders and infrastructure financiers, particularly around transport and energy projects.

frictionVectors.title: South Africa Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports provide vital revenue but deepen structural dependence on South Africa, which remains the dominant market and security partner.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Infrastructure Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Diamond mining and externally financed infrastructure generate foreign exchange but leave the country vulnerable to commodity cycles and outside corporate control.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Gold Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining operations remain central to exports, while weak domestic processing limits Liberia's ability to capture more value from its mineral base.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport Geopolitical Competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and logistics assets attract competing American, European, and Chinese interest, creating bargaining opportunities but also pressure over strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and revenue flows, limiting unified sovereign management of hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain influence through military, energy, and migration interests, constraining Libya's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects attract foreign capital and technology, but Madagascar remains exposed to external operators, commodity volatility, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Rare Earth and Maritime Access
frictionVectors.details: Competition over rare earth prospects, ports, and Indian Ocean connectivity is increasing, giving outside powers leverage over infrastructure and resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and policy conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Malawi's fiscal room remains constrained by debt restructuring and dependence on IMF and other external financing. These lenders strongly influence subsidy, exchange-rate, and public-investment decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic import dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported fuel, fertilizer, and electricity leaves Malawi exposed to foreign-exchange shortages and regional supply disruptions. Transport bottlenecks through neighboring states further weaken sovereign control over essential commodities.

frictionVectors.title: Mining renegotiation and investor conflict
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pursuing a larger state share of gold revenues and tighter control over foreign operators, creating recurring disputes with multinational miners. The approach may increase fiscal capture but risks investment delays and arbitration.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The military government has shifted security cooperation toward Russia and away from Western partners, while counterinsurgency conditions remain severe. Foreign security assistance competes with state institutions for influence over strategic assets and national decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas partnership dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major revenue and energy-security gains but leaves Mauritania reliant on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and coordination with Senegal. Delays or pricing disputes could limit the near-term sovereignty dividend.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridor and local-content pressure
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore expansion and proposed green-hydrogen projects require large external capital commitments and transport infrastructure. Nouakchott must balance investor demands with land, water, employment, and environmental concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty and security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to seek fuller control over the Chagos Archipelago while managing the strategic reality of the Diego Garcia base and UK-US interests. The issue tests the country's ability to convert legal and diplomatic gains into practical sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, telecommunications, and maritime-security ties with India, China, the Gulf, and Western partners create economic opportunities but also strategic balancing risks. Mauritius has generally preserved policy autonomy through diversified partnerships.

highlights: Western Sahara remains strategic fault line

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara diplomacy and resource legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is converting expanding foreign recognition of its autonomy plan into diplomatic and investment leverage, while Algeria and the Polisario Front continue to reject Rabat's position. Phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable projects remain tied to the dispute's legal and political sensitivities.

frictionVectors.title: External capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and US investment supports ports, rail, automotive supply chains, renewables, and green hydrogen. Rabat retains comparatively strong state direction, but competing partners create exposure to geopolitical pressure and technology dependence.

highlights: LNG ambitions remain hostage to Cabo Delgado security
Maputo balances Gulf, Western and Asian capital

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten gas infrastructure, transport routes and the state’s ability to control the province. Foreign military and private-security support remains central to protecting strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Contractual Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms and lenders retain strong leverage over project timelines, revenue structures and security arrangements. Maputo is seeking greater local benefit without deterring capital needed to restart suspended projects.

highlights: Offshore oil discoveries reshape national bargaining power
Green hydrogen plans outpace domestic industrial capacity

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators dominate the capital and technical expertise behind emerging offshore oil projects, creating pressure for stronger local-content and revenue-sharing rules. The government is trying to avoid repeating enclave-extraction patterns seen elsewhere.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Financing
frictionVectors.details: European and Gulf investors are influential in planned hydrogen, ammonia and port projects. Namibia must secure water, power and transport infrastructure while protecting domestic land and energy priorities.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and oil partnerships
Regional isolation raises infrastructure and security costs

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The authorities have reduced Western military involvement and expanded security cooperation with Russia and other non-Western partners. This increases regime autonomy but risks intelligence gaps, sanctions and dependence on opaque external actors.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Oil Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Disputes over uranium concessions and export routes have become symbols of sovereign resource control. Pipeline access, border closures and political tensions with neighbors constrain Niger’s ability to monetize energy assets.

highlights: Fuel reform improves fiscal logic but intensifies social pressure
Oil theft and insecurity erode federal resource control

frictionVectors.title: Oil-Sector Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Production remains constrained by theft, sabotage, aging infrastructure and disputes across operators, communities and regulators. Foreign firms retain major technical and financial influence while the state struggles to convert output into reliable public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf and Western financiers compete for influence through ports, rail, power and digital infrastructure. Financing gaps and debt-service pressures limit Abuja’s bargaining space and can prioritize external repayment over domestic development.

highlights: Kigali preserves tight control over strategic minerals
Regional security policy drives external scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda’s security posture toward eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remains closely linked to accusations involving armed groups and mineral flows. International pressure threatens reputational and economic costs, even as Kigali presents its policy as a sovereignty and security imperative.

frictionVectors.title: Donor and Investment Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda maintains strong state coordination over logistics, technology and mineral value chains, but remains exposed to donor conditionality and foreign investment sentiment. External partners can influence access to finance without directly displacing Kigali’s domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: International firms and neighboring powers are positioning around prospective offshore blocks, while São Tomé lacks the financial and technical capacity to negotiate from a position of strength. Commercial discoveries remain uncertain.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: External financing and security cooperation remain important for port modernization and Gulf of Guinea surveillance, creating modest leverage over national infrastructure choices.

frictionVectors.title: SANGOMAR AND GTA CONTRACT BALANCE
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production gives Dakar greater fiscal space but leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, technology, and financing. Contract transparency, cost recovery, and local participation remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Dakar is seeking infrastructure investment while managing debt and external financing conditions. Gulf, European, Chinese, and multilateral partners compete for influence over logistics and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES ACCESS AND VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access remains economically important but raises concerns over enforcement, sustainability, and whether Seychelles captures enough value from its marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: INDIAN OCEAN SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: India, China, France, and other partners seek maritime access and security cooperation. Victoria must balance surveillance and infrastructure benefits against risks to strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND RUTILE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily exposed to foreign mining capital, commodity prices, and concession terms. The government is pressing for more domestic processing and revenue, but bargaining power remains constrained.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and mining logistics projects can improve connectivity while tying national infrastructure to export corridors and external operators. Transparency and debt sustainability remain central concerns.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE RESOURCE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Federal authorities are promoting offshore oil exploration, but weak regulatory capacity, contested jurisdiction, and insecurity create major risks of foreign leverage and unequal revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, BASES, AND REGIONAL RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, Ethiopia, and other actors compete for access to ports, security partnerships, and trade corridors. These arrangements can support state capacity while deepening fragmentation and external dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and freight-rail failures continue to weaken domestic control over mineral value chains. Private operators and foreign capital are gaining leverage as the state seeks infrastructure investment.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Chinese, Western, and BRICS-linked interest in platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains while trying to retain more processing capacity at home.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence on Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's crude exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving revenue and physical access exposed to armed disruption and external bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented security governance
frictionVectors.details: Political rivalry, incomplete security-sector integration, and local armed competition limit sovereign control over oil regions and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and wartime patronage
frictionVectors.details: Competing military and commercial networks rely on gold, border trade, and external sponsors, diverting resource rents from accountable national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and pipeline disruption
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Port Sudan, oil-export infrastructure, and humanitarian corridors, giving foreign security and logistics actors increased leverage over national access routes.

frictionVectors.title: Gas-contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Potential LNG development could transform state revenues but remains sensitive to fiscal terms, local-content obligations, and the negotiating power of international energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors are attracting Gulf, Chinese, and Western investment, creating growth opportunities alongside concerns over long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's container, transit, and phosphate economy depends heavily on external finance and regional trade flows, limiting domestic leverage over key logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and insecurity near the northern frontier threaten transport routes and public spending, while regional security partnerships expand outside influence over border management.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited access to concessional finance leaves Tunisia vulnerable to leverage from European partners and Gulf-linked lenders. Fiscal pressure constrains independent energy and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Mediterranean energy exposure
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported gas and electricity, alongside delayed renewable projects, weakens control over strategic energy security. Phosphate-sector disruption further reduces export resilience.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil corridor remains central to national revenue plans but faces environmental criticism, financing constraints, and pressure from Western institutions. Chinese participation provides an alternative but increases long-term infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security costs
frictionVectors.details: Operations against armed groups and regional military commitments consume fiscal resources and deepen reliance on external security partnerships. Instability around eastern Congo and South Sudan threatens transport and trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership contest
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking greater fiscal returns, processing capacity, and transparency from multinational copper operators while courting US, European, and Gulf capital. The need for investment limits its bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and power infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved policy space but leaves Zambia exposed to creditor conditions and refinancing risk. Electricity shortages threaten mining output and increase dependence on regional power imports.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, while Harare seeks domestic processing and stronger state capture of rents. Weak governance and opaque contracts risk converting mineral wealth into limited public benefit.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to international finance raise transaction costs and push Zimbabwe toward Chinese, Russian, and regional channels. This diversification increases maneuvering room but can reduce transparency and competitive leverage.
